utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Maria Naumceska, who is from the Republic of Macedonia and has been with my team since November of last year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, I note that counsel for Mr. Beara, Mr. Ostojic, is in the courtroom. Good morning to you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today, Mr. Beara, you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. I like to remind you that the oath you took is still valid. And I take it, Mr. Ostojic, the Chamber doesn't need to repeat the Rule 90(E) advice for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I believe you don't have to, but from time to time Mr. Beara may ask for it, so depending on the questions, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Good morning, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Beara, you are serving a life sentence; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the last judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This Tribunal found you beyond a reasonable doubt guilty of persecution through murder and cruel inhumane treatment, guilty of murder, guilty of extermination, guilty of genocide; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the finding of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And many of your associates in the VRS security administration have been convicted. Your superior, Tolimir, also convicted of genocide in another trial. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All that is well-known.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Security officer below you in the Drina Corps, Popovic, also convicted of genocide?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You know that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to remind you of one question and one answer you gave in your evidence in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now I can read out the question in open session, Your Honours, but I'll have to read out the answer in private session, so perhaps if you're bear with me I'll read out the question. So in response to the question on the last occasion: "During the war, did you ever author or read any VRS document that indicated that prisoners from Srebrenica would be, were being, or had been executed? You gave the following answer which we'll hear in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You gave this answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "I never authored an order of that kind, nor did I ever see such an order in a written form. It is also true that nobody ever orally ordered me any such thing nor did I hear anybody order anybody else any such thing." You never gave, received, or heard any orders to execute prisoners from Srebrenica. That is not an honest answer, is it, Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an honest answer. You should know that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do you recall what the Trial Chamber in your case said about you? And let me read out a passage from the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Can we go back into public session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear from -- you're not asking to lift the confidentiality of the previous question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not at this time, but I think that this question can be asked in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think so. Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: There's no reason why the question can't be asked in public session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do you recall what the Trial Chamber in your case said about you? I'm going to quote from your judgement at paragraph 2165. Said this: "As chief of security in the VRS Main Staff, cloaked with the authority of Mladic, he gave directions and orders to the subordinate troops who implemented the murder plan. It was the abuse of this senior position within the VRS which allowed him to utilise the resources at his disposal to orchestrate the crimes." Do you recall the Trial Chamber's finding to that effect in your case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I don't remember. Who would remember? That was almost two years ago. But I remember that a telegram was shown from the chief of the public security centre, Dragomir Vasic, where he writes that the MUP had taken over assignments from the army, that it surrounded and liquidated 8.000 Muslims. And that was later --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the verb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat from where you referred to 8.000 Muslims? The interpreters didn't hear you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, I can. It's a telegram written by Dragomir Vasic, chief of the public security centre at Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: What are you pulling out of your folder, please, on your desk?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: What are you pulling out and putting on the folder on your desk?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's papers. It's not a gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Would you put it, please, back? Would you put it back, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why? That's what I'm talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may object, and I'm not sure if I have right to object. I just think the Prosecution, will all due respect, doesn't have a right to direct the witness as to what he should do. I think perhaps the request should be directed to the Chamber, and if the Court believes he can't refer to rely on things, then so be it, the Court will direct Mr. Beara, but I think it's unfair for the Prosecution to sternly direct any witness, particularly a witness that was subpoenaed by this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it should be correct on the part of the witness to ask permission from the Bench before he consults any documents, in the circumstances in which we do not know what that document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that, Your Honour. I think the confusion, and I'm not -- I think when he was asked to restate it, he was trying to refresh his recollection because he didn't catch fully what he stated about the document that he was referencing, so needs to apparently rely on it. So he looked at it in order to answer fully the question by the Chamber. In any event, I would object to the OTP's instructions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Beara, I would appreciate if could you answer the question from your memory, and, if necessary, ask permission from the Bench to consult the document to refresh your memory. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I understand, and I'm sorry that I rifled through my papers. At any rate, I said that this telegram exists which is in the evidence in the case, a telegram from Dragomir Vasic, chief of the public security centre of Zvornik who is linked to the Ministry of Interior, saying that, due to the engagement of the VRS in the operation concerning Zepa, the MUP forces took over assignments from the army, and that they surrounded and liquidated 8.000 Muslims. That's what I wanted to say. That document was shown during the trial, and later in some magical way, disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Beara --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- I'm not asking about that specific documents in your case. I meant to ask you, please, another -- I'm going ask you and remind you of another passage in your Trial Chamber's judgement about you, what they said in finding you guilty of genocide. It's paragraph 1318 of the judgement. They said this: "The factors which the Trial Chamber finds to be decisive in finding that Beara had the requisite specific intent for genocide are the scale and scope of the killing operation carried out with his knowledge pursuant to his instructions and under his supervision, his extensive and forceful participation in all components of the killing operation, his demonstrated determination to kill as many as possible and his vital contribution in overcoming hurdles and challenges to effective implementation. Further, the systematic, exclusive targeting of Bosnian Muslims, the repetition by Beara of destructive and discriminatory acts and his words all evidence his genocidal intent. Further, his participation in these killings with knowledge that they would contribute to the destruction of the group also demonstrates his genocidal intent. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that Beara participated in the JCE to murder with genocidal intent. He is therefore guilty of genocide." You don't accept that finding?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept it at all. It is, indeed, written, but that's not how it happened in that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You don't --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have led evidence to that effect, but, again, I say all that we presented disappeared in some magical way. Why and how, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The Prosecutor is reading some paragraphs from the judgement and interpreters don't have the text of the judgement at their disposal at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We can have it at 65 ter 25863. I wasn't going to bring it up, but it's available there. Paragraph 1318 that I just read is an English page, 532; B/C/S, page 535. I'm just going to refer to one other small portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But please read it very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I will do. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Trial Chamber found -- and this is at paragraph 1068, it found this: "It found that the heavy hand of the security branch was evident throughout -- throughout, that is the killing operations. Beara, they said, was at the centre of the killing operations with Popovic and together you were responsible for overall planning and implementation logistics, locations, personnel." That's what they found. They said that you translated the murder plan into actions. That is, together in Zvornik, Beara, Popovic, and Nikolic translated the murder plan into actions. That is an accurate statement of your role in the Srebrenica events, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know, in fact, what you're asking me. Do you want me to confirm that I orchestrated the murders?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In your final trial brief, in your own trial, you denied all knowledge at the time of the crimes perpetrated following the fall of Srebrenica. Is that a position you maintain?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber for permission to get a paper out of my file regarding these allegations of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness just answer my question. He's answered the question. I've got another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the question was whether you denied all knowledge at the time of the crimes in your final brief, in your own trial. I think can you answer the question without having to rely on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, he has done. He said, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not have known anything about that at the time because I was not in the field. However, some other people were in the field, and you can see that from the intercepts where Pavle and Vuk are talking about it, and this Pavle on our side, who later very persistently and constantly claimed that I and my men had been organisers of the killings and he knew nothing about it, he is calling members of the Muslim unit that came behind the Zvornik Brigade lines. He is saying, I'll kill you in the woods, 100 men for one, and if that's not clear to you, go to Orahovac and surrender. He didn't go -- he didn't say, Go to Beara and surrender; he said, Go to Orahovac. And Orahovac is an execution site, if somebody doesn't know it. That's what I heard during the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Beara, I'm not asking about your analysis of the evidence in your trial, just about you. You -- you maintain then -- wait, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are analysing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Wait, please. You raise an alibi Defence in your trial - I think you just referred to it - you said that you were in Belgrade between the 13th and 14th. Is that something you still maintain? 13th and 14th of July obviously. Yes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak much closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I said of course I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Beara, you are requested by the interpreter to come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do you deny that thousands of men -- we don't need to be specific about the numbers. Thousands of men were systematically murdered by Bosnian Serb forces following the fall of Srebrenica. That's what your Trial Chamber found. Do you deny that, the truth of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I deny the horrible things that happened in that civil war, religious war? It is a curse, not warfare. What happened was horrific --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You recall --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- terrifying. But in some magical way, in some mysterious way, it was all pinned on three men from the security service of the VRS, men who neither had the authority or subordinates who were murders and prepared to kill. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Trial Chamber found that you were omnipresent in the Zvornik area, the scene of the mass killings in the Zvornik area. You would reject that finding too?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That's another mysterious or magical turn that this affair took. The Prosecution witnesses who were called to testify to my presence, or the documents presented to the Court and admitted into evidence, were of such a nature that it's simply difficult to believe because these witnesses always see me alone at this execution site, staring into the distance, lost in my own thoughts, or they see me walking about and then they say -- or, rather, somebody tells them, This is Beara. But you never brought the person who told them that this person was Beara. You only brought the people who recognised me, looking at my back, but you never brought that person who told the witnesses that who they were looking at was Beara. There was this nurse who provided bandages somewhere to tie the hands of people who were being taken to be executed also said she had seen me at the execution site. But the way she put it, it was the investigator who gave her my name. What she actually said was that she had seen some lieutenant-colonel or colonel, and then she described me in various ways and then the investigator says, Could it be Beara? And she replies, Yes, it could be. I know that Beara from the Drina Corps, from the time when I was in the Drina Corps. And that's one of the cases. There were more of the same kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I've got no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pack. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Excellency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Beara. The Chamber would like to thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say one more thing, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Beara, what do you want to say to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to say this: When our trial was nearing the end, you were on the Trial Chamber, some people spoke at the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Beara --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- you were examined by the accused and cross-examined by the Prosecution. I think that's it. I -- I thought you would say some words of usual things. I appreciate it. And I also thank Mr. Ostojic for his co-operation and assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may be excused Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I go now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness was scheduled for a little bit later because of the estimate, so if we could take a break and as soon as he arrives -- he was told to arrive at 10.00, I think he may be here a little earlier but if we can take a break until he arrives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break for half an hour? We will resume at 10.00. We will have some shorter break afterwards. Hearing adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 9.28 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, the Chamber asked you to return to the courtroom because there was one thing that I wanted to deal with in your presence. That's about the request of Mr. Robinson to lift the confidentiality of the part of evidence Mr. Beara gave in private session. So shall I hear from the Prosecution first whether it is in the position to make observation about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's a very fair formulation whether we're in a position or not, and, in fact, my response implicates the question you were about to ask Mr. Ostojic because we had a discussion at the break. I had actually envisaged that this issue would be resolved somewhat later in the proceedings for various reasons, but under these circumstances, given the stage of the proceedings for the witness, the nature of the testimony, and most particularly the fact that I now know that Mr. Beara, Mr. Ostojic do not object. In that case, the Prosecution does not either. But, of course, you'll need to hear from Mr. Ostojic but I couldn't respond to the Court without alluding to the discussion we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We have -- I have consulted with Mr. Beara, and we do not have an objection to lifting the confidentiality that you raised, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we bring the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, in light of the submission of the parties and counsel for Mr. Bera, we hereby lift the confidentiality of Mr. Bera's evidence given in private session, as well as the audio/video part of the proceedings. Of course, that includes the part of today's hearing that was given -- conducted in private session as well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let us just take this slowly and let us pause. You were asked -- or, rather, it was suggested to you that links with Pale were better than what you had said. A decision on mobilisation was shown here. Did you see many documents before the corridor came to exist? How many documents from Pale did you examine at the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I, quite simply, forgot. I mean, this document too. But I don't remember that there were any documents or contacts, and I said yesterday that, as far as I'm concerned, there weren't any contacts. I think that we worked more on the basis of our own knowledge rather than some instructions that could not have arrived from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We submitted a document here from my diary when I met people from Prijedor on the first page -- or, rather, in the first sentence it says: "In relation to the 30th of May, the first 45 days without contact with us." How does that tally with your experience?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was. If it was recorded as such, that is certainly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D435, could that briefly be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a record from a session of our government held on the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page, please. The penultimate one in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a blockade in the Krajina. Could you tell us, please, third from the bottom, that a helicopter is requested from the army and the government would use that. And then the next one says to do away with the blockade of the Bosanska Krajina, and the last one, the government decided to take all measures, including military measures, to deblockade the Bosnian Krajina and ensure regular food supplies and other goods for the region? Did the government have a basis for taking this kind of position with regard to developments in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were in a very awkward position. We were sealed off as far as Serbia was concerned. And, on the other side, the Cazin Krajina was armed and always prepared to attack Prijedor because they always thought that that was part of Muslim territory. The situation in the Krajina was such that there was barely any food, basic supplies. Also, there was a shortage of medicine. We know of the case of the 12 babies. Let me not go into all of that now. How do I put this? Some people were careless and that made that happen. And the international community could have made a step in that direction at least through the Red Cross, in order to ensure some medicine. Of course, certain activities were taken to open the corridor which was a life-line for the Serb people, in order for the Serb people to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the Crisis Staff or other authorities in Prijedor whether they had resources and then deprived the population and detainees of that intentionally, and without any reason, food, medicine energy, other resources --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness has made clear that he had very little to do with the detention facilities. So before asking about depriving detainees of food, et cetera, a foundational question should be asked about the witness's knowledge about these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to leave that aside. I'm going to withdraw that as regards detainees. I'm talking about the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff do everything it could or they -- or did they intentionally deprive the population of something that they could have provided to them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Crisis Staff never denied anything. In accordance with our abilities, we provided food to the population, regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was commander of civilian protection, ex officio, then together with the Red Cross, and that was within my purview, in fact, wherever necessary as far as bread, flour, milk, diary products were concerned, we provided that to the population - and how do I put this? - to the collection centre of Trnopolje and persons who did not have food at home, et cetera. So irrespective of ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you mentioned a neighbouring village. However, we did not make it possible for you to finish. A Muslim village that was in the neighbourhood that was well armed, what was the name of that village? What happened to it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Hambarine, the village of Carakovo, Zecovi. So that is the belt above Tukovi where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether other Muslim villages, those that had handed over their weapons, whether they were attacked, whether they had any fighting there Suha, Vapolje [phoen]. Can you remember some others that were not involved in any kind of fighting?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the village of Cela. There was no fighting there; that is to say, people were loyal. They handed over their weapons. As a matter of fact, I think that they even removed extremists from their area. They didn't want to have any contact with them. For example, one part is called Muslim Gomjenica. Also in Tukovi, too. There were no problem there. To this day, people live there. I mean, they were refugee for a while but they came back to their homes and that's where they live now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Muslimanska Gomjenica that is not reflected in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Muslimanska Gomjenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Gomjenica?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call it Gomjenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about this village of Cela, how big is that? What's the population?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not very good like this. But like all the other villages, Carakovo, Hambarine, so all of these villages are roughly -- well, it's very densely populated. Like Hambarine, Cela has a densely populated centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this depended on, whether there would be any fighting in a village? Did it depend on whether they would be attacked or what?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the will of the population that lived there. The Muslim population, I mean. If they were really in favour of life and peace, remaining there in that area as neighbours, there was no problem whatsoever. Even those who left asked their neighbours to take care of their homes, you see? There were people who asked me to take care of their houses. However, I was so busy that I could not take care of anybody's house. I mean, I cannot be at work and take care of somebody's house, but there were people who were not working and who were neighbours and who took care of their other neighbours' homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask permission to re-cross-examine on one point which was relating to the Muslim villages that -- the answer about the Muslim villages for where there were no problems such as the village of Cela. I'd like to show the witness one document and ask one question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have P3852, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is, as you can see, a security assessment for Prijedor municipality by the SMB in Banja Luka dated the 23rd of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph, it refers to: The national division reached its climax in armed conflicts between the Serbian people which had taken power and the Muslim and Croat extremists on the other. The next line down, it says: Dozens of villages have been almost completely destroyed and left uninhabited. And then there's a long list of villages. And then it says: Or partly destroyed. And there's another long list of village, including the village of Cela. Now, that is the village which you claimed a moment ago -- for which you claimed a moment ago there were no problems there to this day, people lived there; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment when all of this was happening in May and June 1992, I talked about that, afterwards, these people asked to leave, and they did leave. However, some neighbours took care of their houses whereas others devastated their houses and sold things from them. Many people returned to Cela and live there to this day. Somebody should investigate that and see that that is indeed the case. Once a house is abandoned, it is very hard to take care of it, to protect it from anyone, any citizen. People drove tractors, carried rifles, took off windows, doors, whatever. They'd come from a different municipality altogether and do that. It was very hard to prevent that. So when a house is empty, then -- well, that's why the Crisis Staff said that abandoned property should be declared socially owned property so that people would realise that this should not be touched because it is state-owned property.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So it's true, is it -- is it not, that the village of Cela was partly destroyed, as this document says?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly destroyed, in terms of construction facilities, not on the basis of war-time activity, but on the basis of peace-time activity by the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just ask that we focus additionally, just on one part of paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The one that's on the screen. It says: As these people left, there began a massive looting of their property which was left entirely unguarded by either the owners or the municipal authorities. The impotence of the official authorities to do anything about this could be felt at that time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Mandic, how does this tally with your own experience? Did the authorities view this looting favourably?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this paragraph, Mr. President, because it is responsive to the question put by the lady, the Prosecutor. We never viewed this favourably. Quite simply, the situation was such that I personally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The times were such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that these were very difficult times. I didn't even dare watch what my neighbour was doing and see what he was bringing from some Muslim village. This would lead to poor neighbourly relations and other consequences. But we, in the Crisis Staff, took other measures, and we asked the organs of the civilian police, the military police, to protect these buildings as best they could. Since a front line was opened towards the corridor, many conscripts had to go to the front line and, quite simply, those who even promised that they would take care of the houses did not manage to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is it your evidence, Mr. Mandic, that the partial destruction in the village of Cela was due to construction works which took place after the people left?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Devastation by the population that had stayed on, the Serb population, not because of war activity. It wasn't that somebody used tanks to destroy that. It was the people themselves who devastated these houses and then took the material back to build their own houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the last sentence of the paragraph in which Cela was mentioned, which you saw earlier on, says like this, I quote: "This destruction saw the beginning of mass exodus of both Muslims and Croats." Is it consistent with your memory, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People started moving out even before that. People started moving out of Prijedor already in February, March, April. First it was women, children, and the elderly who took buses and tried to leave in some way. And the extremists stayed on in Prijedor and, of course, if somebody went into the wood, their house would remain empty, and such a house could not be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Mandic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next witness is Mr. Sipovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sipovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Sipovac.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please let us take care to leave a short pause between questions and answers and speak more slowly. We are from Herzegovina and speak very fast but then we have problems with the interpretation. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9663 is the document I would like to show the witness in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the screen. The Serbian version is on the left side. Do you see your statement?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I see a part of it; three paragraphs on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. But I should now like to ask you about these words, "To establish the VTO." It's paragraph 3, line 3. It says: "To establish the VTO," but it should actually be, "to man, or to fill the VTO," because the establishment was decided by a previous decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, you mean that the VTOs that had been formed earlier were filled with personnel?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you want to make the correction that this text should read: "The earlier formed VTOs were filled with personnel"?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the rest of the statement faithfully reflect what you've told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: On page 2, there is a typo. It's not the "VP 3673," but "VP 3670," and later, it should be "VP 3662."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you want to repeat that?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Page 2, line 3, the number should change. "3670" and later "7362."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the rest of the statement correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Paragraph 10. It's not year "1992" but it's "1991." Line 1 of that sentence. I cannot remember the date, but it's "1991," not "1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that page 4 in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you just want to change the year from "1992" into "1991"?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. From what I can see, the rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the last page so the witness can identify his signature. [In English] Last page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put to you the same questions today as those asked by the members of my Defence team, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Essentially I would not change anything. I would only provide additional explanation, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tendered this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objections, Ms. Iodice [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Pelic, Your Honours. And good morning, Your Honours. No objection. However, we would like to note that some of the questions in this statement are formulated in a leading fashion and also some of them invite the witness to draw conclusions on legal issues; for instance, questions 6, 12, 13 and 14 are obviously leading questions and the last three are also asking for witness to draw legal conclusions so that should go to the weight of the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies, Ms. Pelic. Sometimes that happens. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4230, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read a brief summary of Mr. Cedo Sipovac's statement in English. [In English] Cedo Sipovac was an official in the Secretariat for the People's Defence in Prijedor. Cedo Sipovac noticed in 1991 that the political situation in Yugoslavia was becoming more complicated and that the constitution and orders of the SFRY Presidency were not being fully respected. This was highlighted when instructions arrived from the Republican Secretariat for the National Defence in BH which banned the secretariats from mobilising war units. However, in the same document, instructions were provided for how to carry out the mobilisation. To Cedo Sipovac's knowledge, all appointments and replacements in the JNA were done in accordance with the regulations valid at the time and that there was no planned replacement of personnel. He noted that people of all ethnicities responded to the call-up in 1991. Cedo Sipovac does not agree with the claims of witnesses that Muslims were issued with inferior weapons and that the Serbs with automatic rifles is not correct. Cedo Sipovac recalls that at some point in 1992, a crowd gathered in the front of the building of the Secretariat of National Defence in Prijedor, which, to his knowledge, had been organised by the Patriotic League. They wished to take the documentation from the secretariat to avoid their use for the call-up of conscripts. Further, on 30th May, 1992, he is aware that the Muslims attacked the urban area of Prijedor and several members of the army and police were wounded, some killed. Cedo Sipovac was not aware of the Crisis Staffs, any civilian authorities, or the police in the municipalities serving as an engine or means for the permanent removal through genocide, persecution, extermination, murders, deportations and inhumane acts of Bosnian Muslims and Croats from those territories of BH to which the Serbs laid claim. Cedo Sipovac was not aware of any camps in the Prijedor area. He knew of two investigation centres in Omarska and Keraterm. He was also aware of a collection centre in Trnopolje where people voluntarily visited and stayed until they left Prijedor because they felt unsafe. And at that moment, I do not have additional questions for Mr. Sipovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sipovac, as you have noted that your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing; that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. But when Mr. Karadzic read out this here, he repeated that year, 1992. But it's actually 1991. I'm sorry to make this correction again, but it's really wrong in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate it very much. Thank you. And, Mr. Sipovac, I like -- I wanted to tell you that at any moment when you feel uncomfortable, please let us know. We'll take a break whenever necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pelic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipovac, first, I would really briefly like to deal with the roles that you had and to clarify that issue. According to the paragraph 2 of your statement, from September 1984 until October 1991, you worked at the Secretariat of National Defence in Prijedor as a clerical officer for civil protection; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpretation just began with the words "September 1984," and I didn't hear what you said before that. So I heard in my headset the part where you say "from September 1984," but what exactly? Could you repeat that? I didn't hear the entire interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: No problem I will repeat again. I would very briefly like to clarify the roles that you had. According to the paragraph 2 of your statement, from September 1984 until October 1991, you worked at the Secretariat of National Defence in Prijedor as a clerical officer for civilian protection; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And in your statement, you repeatedly state that you were a clerical officer for the recruitment and mobilisation of conscripts under the military territorial organ, which is also short as VTO. Sir, but, in fact, you were not just a clerical officer. You were the chief of the military territorial organ for mobilisation at the Prijedor garrison, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No, I was not the chief. I was the assistant. At VTO, I was never a chief. The chief was Major Mile Stojanovic; he was chief of section. And my direct superior in affairs of mobilisation was Captain Micic. I worked there in that section from September 1984 until August 1992, at the VTO, if you're talking about the VTO.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: You know Slavko Budimir, who, starting from the take-over of Prijedor on 30th of April, 1992, was the secretary of the municipal Secretariat for National Defence, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up 65 ter 25872.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 1 -- transcript page 12859, lines 17 and 18. Transcript page 12859. This is the testimony of Slavko Budimir in the Prosecutor versus Stakic case, and when asked about your role, Mr. Budimir testified that you were the chief of the VTO for mobilisation at the Prijedor garrison. And that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Probably the witness doesn't understand English and you better tell the witness what this is about. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would be objecting to any reference to this transcript or the testimony of Mr. Budimir, because we have made a -- a motion for a subpoena for Mr. Budimir to be a Defence witness. And on the 22nd of January, 2013, the decision on accused's motion to subpoena Slavko Budimir, the Trial Chamber denied that motion. So we think it's unfair for the Prosecution to be able to use any portion of Mr. Budimir's evidence without us having had the right to bring him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you expand on the reason why it would be unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Because we have asked for Mr. Budimir to come and testify, probably he already would have testified, and then we would have had a chance -- or any issues about his position about this witness's position or anything he said to have been fully explored. But now if you allow the Prosecution to use this evidence without us having been able to call the witness, even though this may be a minor point in principle, we don't believe that the Prosecution should be able to use evidence from witnesses who we were denied the opportunity to call. You might recall this came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can understand your objection if the Prosecution is minded to tender this document. This was -- the transcript into evidence, but she is just putting the question about witness's position at the time, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, she's making use of evidence that essentially is not available to us. So in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand that this is not available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the witness and his evidence is not available to us because we tried to call this witness and you denied us the right to call him. That's my point. This issue came up once before with respect to Mr. Tomo Sivic [phoen], a military judge whose document was attempted to be used, and you denied the subpoena and you allowed the Prosecution to proceed. But I wanted to maintain our objection, if nothing else but in principle, that when a witness is not available to us because the Chamber denied a subpoena, the Prosecution ought not to be able to ask questions about events involving that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But would you like to make any observations, Ms. Pelic? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I, Mr. President. First, may I respectfully suggest that when Mr. Robinson knows that the issue has been ruled on before, that if he wants simply to maintain his objection, which is really not necessary, I believe. We crossed that road before. He acknowledges that the Trial Chamber has expressed its opinion on this issue and simply notes that, rather than impliedly seek reconsideration without acknowledging that until the Trial Chamber presses him on the issue. Secondly, apart from the fact that the Trial Chamber has ruled on it, the Trial Chamber's ruling was perfectly correct. The observations that you made this morning, Mr. President, underpin that. Let's hear what the witness has to say. His position may very well be, That's exactly right. And we either get further evidence and information which -- to which this Court is entitled, or we prevent a witness from being able to testify contrary to information that has been elicited in this institution before, without knowledge of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger's observation. There's no difficulty at all with the Prosecution putting this transcript to the witness. Please -- please continue, Ms. Pelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipovac, Slavko Budimir testified in the Prosecutor versus Stakic case, and I will quote now. When asked about your role,

utterances.speaker: MR. BUDIMIR TESTIFIED
utterances.text: "He was the chief of the military territorial organ for mobilisation at the Prijedor garrison." That's correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. And in my previous answer, I said that I was never the chief of the military territorial organ in Prijedor. The chief was Milivoj Stojanovic and his assistant for mobilisation was, I believe, Captain Jovan Micic. That was a long time ago, and I was a desk officer working on mobilisation affairs at the VTO in Prijedor, and that organ covered the area of Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanska Dubica, and Novi Grad. Those are the municipalities covered by the VTO based in Prijedor. I don't think I need to repeat this anymore because I have already given a solemn declaration to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. I don't know why Mr. Budimir stated something like this. I did not expect such questions so I did not bring my personal documentation, and I could have, because I have all my letters of appointment. I can provide them to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Very well. You acknowledge in your statement under question number 9 that you attended the 15th of May, 1992, meeting of the Council for National Defence of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly where you reported on the mobilisation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I'm not sure it was on the 15th because in some previous trials, Defence teams told me that my name was mentioned as one of those present. I don't remember it, but I was present perhaps only in situations when briefing was provided on mobilisation, otherwise I would not attend. But these meetings discussing national defence discussed issues of mobilisation, which was very topical at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up P03529. And can I correct the transcript: P03529.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, these are the -- the minutes of the 4th meeting of the Council for National Defence of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly held on 15th of May, 1992, that I just mentioned to you. And if you look at the list of people attending, you will see your name noted as present. That's correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Cedo Sipovac, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And if you look at the agenda, under item 2, it's "mobilisation in the municipality."

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And if we could go in English on the page 2, please, and B/C/S, it's still page 1. Last paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, your name is mentioned there as one of the persons involved in the discussion on the mobilisation in the Prijedor municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. It says "conclusions." We're still on the first page. The proposal -- the proposed decision on the organisation and functioning of the Crisis Staff is accepted with a proviso that the proposed composition of the staff is supplemented with the representative of the garrison, Prijedor. Yes. And then we -- yes, mobilisation and then I see my name. Sorry, I took time to read this text. Yes, the last in the third line is my name. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And this is, indeed, the meeting that we are discussing on the 15th of May, 1992, at which you reported on the mobilisation; correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Probably. I had no other role in that, except to discuss the carrying out of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And this mobilisation that happened in May 1992 in the Prijedor municipality was conducted pursuant to the decision of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I did not receive any interpretation. I can't understand English, and I did not receive any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you receiving translation now?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That mobilisation was not ordered by the autonomous region. Mobilisation was an ongoing process, which started in 1991, and it lasted for as long as the need to replenish war units existed. It went on throughout 1991 and 1992. I'm not familiar with any orders. The only order I am familiar with was the order that was issued on the 21st of May. That process was ongoing. It was a process that went on uninterruptedly. I really don't know what mobilisation order you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes: The word was "uninterruptedly."

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up P03535.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, these are the minutes of the second session of the National Defence Council of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor held on 5th of May, 1992. If you could please take a look at a conclusion number 2, it's on page 1, both in English and B/C/S. It states and I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we see his name here as being present?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: No, he was not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I will quote the conclusion number 2: "The mobilisation orders following from the decision of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina Assembly are to be carried out, when the actual situation in the municipality renders it necessary, in accordance with requirements and a special plan, through call-up papers issued by the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence." And, in fact, this just shows that mobilisation was carried out pursuant to the decision of the Autonomous Region Bosanska Krajina Assembly, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: You're asking me something that we can read here. But I was not in charge of mobilisation. I didn't participate in that mobilisation. I did not receive any such decisions or order either from the chief or anybody else. This was a position of the council which considered mobilisation, and it was its right. I don't know how it happened. This is what you're saying. This is what I read here, but I don't know. I can't comment upon this because I don't know. I didn't -- I don't know. I didn't participate in that. I didn't work on that. I told you when I received the mobilisation order on the 21st of May, 2002 [as interpreted], that was an order for general mobilisation, which I received from my superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: But on the 15th of May, 1992, you were at the meeting, the fourth meeting of this council, and you reported on the mobilisation. You just confirmed that, and that's the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Madam, I confirmed that, and I repeat -- I repeat mobilisation was a continuous process. It was an ongoing process from the moment when received a -- a mobilisation signal. It went on until there was a need to replenish war units. It started in 1991 and went on throughout 1992, 1993, 1994, and so on and so forth. I told you what I knew; i.e., I shared with you the information that I had about the situation on the ground, and this is what I stand by. But this was not done pursuant to this decision but, rather, pursuant to the requirements of the units. And I apologise for using the word "insist," but you insist upon me telling that this was what I had in my hands, but, no, I didn't. That was never issued to me from my superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I will move to another topic that I wish to discuss with you. In your statement, under questions 5 and 6, you stated that you don't have any facts about anyone replacing Muslim officers by Serbian officers, including replacement of Colonel Muharem Efendic by Serbian officer Colonel Vladimir Radisic, in "a planned fashion with a purpose." Let's look at a couple of examples. On the day of the take-over of Prijedor, 30th of April, 1992, secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence, Becir Medunjanin, was replaced by Slavko Budimir, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: According to you, yes; and according to the documents that I have, yes. I didn't know about that, but that had nothing whatsoever to do with what I did. I was a member of the armed forces of the JNA, and I can tell you that had nothing whatsoever to do with anything. I apologise. Don't switch off my microphone. That had nothing to do with the part of the armed forces and the army. That was the Secretariat for National Defence which was in charge of civilian structures and here we're talking about the issue whether there were any shakeups in the army. I'm claiming that there were no shakeups in the army, as far as I know, and when I was appointed chief, that was never done. And there are actually examples to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, Becir Medunjanin was a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: It is not a pleasant thing to talk about somebody's ethnic affiliations without that person confirming that, but I will accept what you say, that he was a Muslim. I know Becir Medunjanin personally and that's why I say what I do. I used to know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And, indeed, Slavko Budimir was a Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: You said he was. Well, I suppose he still is. I don't know whether he changed his ethnic affiliations. But I'm telling you that it is not a good thing to comment upon somebody's ethnic affiliations without consulting with that person first.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Well, also Vahid Ceric was dismissed from the post of assistant commander for the organisation of mobilisation and personnel affairs by the Executive Committee of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor on 5th of May, 1992, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Madam, your basic question was about the army, and I told you that there were no such things in the army, i.e., in war units. What you're asking me now are questions that pertain to civilian structures. If you're talking about the executive board, that was within its purview. It was not within the purview of the JNA or the army. It was within the purview of the structures, and I really can't comment upon that because it is not pleasant for me to comment on that because I wasn't there. I did not participate in that process. If there were any such things - I suppose that there were - there must be a document to that effect, but that had nothing to do with my job. It had nothing to do with war units, with the JNA, and armed forces, and this was done within the purview of civilian structures. That was what they did. And why things like that were done, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up P03554.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the Serbian municipality of Prijedor Executive Committee decision dated 5th of May, 1992, signed by the president of the Executive Committee, Dr. Milan Kovacevic. Item 1 of this decision states that Vahid Ceric is dismissed from his post. And item 2 states that Major Radmilo Zeljaja shall be responsible for the implementation of this decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Asked and answered. The witness does not know anything about what was going on in the civilian structure of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He might be refreshed by this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And I haven't asked my question yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please -- please continue. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, Major Radmilo Zeljaja who was in charge of implementing this decision that we are looking at was in the 43rd Motorised Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: According to this decision, that was the case. I'm not a lawyer but this is a confusion of authorities. Zeljaja couldn't deal with that. I am familiar with this part of a job, given what I did. I don't know why something drafted this. I won't go into that. But this should not have been written. The executive board, and I can explain, I'm not a lawyer by profession but I can see that these are two totally different bodies which have nothing whatsoever to do with each other. The president of the executive board is under the authority of civilian structures and the Assembly. And what about the authorities of the TO? The civilian structures appointed employees and officers in TO Staffs, and Radmilo Zeljaja, who was a major and who was my commander and my superior later on, had nothing to do with that. The army and -- and the civilian structures could not overlap. If it happened later, then, yes. But since it happened when it did, knowing what I did from -- knowing what I knew from practice, and formally and legally these are two completely different bodies. You can't be tasked with doing something if you're in the army, and to be tasked with things such as appointments. Those were within the purview of civilian structure. And Vahid Ceric, whom I know, worked in the TO Staff. He was one of the officers in the TO, and Radmila Zeljaja was in the JNA, and there the authorities are completely different.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters are kindly asking you to slow down when you're providing your answers.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. I can repeat, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat the answer. So, contrary to your position, this is one more example of replacement based on ethnicity, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: For the third time, I repeat. I do not want to provide such comments here because it is not a proper thing to talk about somebody's ethnic affiliations based on names. It may be done in some cultures but I'm not willing to do that. There were no examples in the army where I worked of such a nature. If you want me to provide evidence to the contrary, I can. Such things didn't happen. I don't want to comment upon this. I don't want to say, I don't want to confirm that this was based on ethnic affiliations. I don't want to comment upon that because I cannot recognise that pattern in that, because you can't say that this was based on ethnic affiliations. Please. Tell me if you can, why do you think that it was done on ethnic affiliations? Because Vahid is Vahid? I don't see any explanation. I don't see a statement of reasons that would point to that fact. And I can't confirm your assertion that this was done based on ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, Vahid Ceric is a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Madam, you are persistent. You're trying to convince me of something that I can't accept. I can understand that you are judging by the name, but I don't see it in the document. I knew Vahid, I worked with him, I co-operated with him, but I don't want to -- to approach the problem in such a way. I cannot confirm that he was removed because he was a Muslim. I don't know that he was a Muslim. I don't know whether he declared himself as a Muslim. I have never held in my hands any document in which it says that he, himself, declared as a Muslim. If you ask me similar questions in the future, then I can share with you my own personal reasons for believing that you are wrong and why this is not so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to deal with the last topic. In your statement, pages 6 to 8, you stated that you have no knowledge about the crimes that happened in the Prijedor municipality, according to the indictment in this case. You also stated that had this had been the policy of the civilian or police authorities at a local or municipal level, the defence structures would have known about it. Well, this Trial Chamber has received a large amount of evidence of the crimes committed in the Prijedor municipality. We just talked about replacement of your colleague, Becir Medunjanin. The Trial Chamber has heard the evidence that he was tortured and killed in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court and the accused, that can be found at confidential P00707, transcript page 2728 and 2730 to 2738.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are aware of the fate of the head of the organisation that you used to work for, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I am aware of it from what you have told me. I really didn't know about that before. What I would say as a human being about him that he was very fair in dealings with myself. In terms of humanity, he was very fair in the dealings with me. I'm sorry that he ended up like that. I didn't know. Sometimes when I watch television I hear the family name Medunjanin, and I thought that I might get in contact with that man because I thought that that may be his son who plays football. He was chief of secretariat when I left the secretariat, and he was very fair when he offered me to help -- that he would help me if I had any problems. He was a very fair person, and I'm sorry that he ended up the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, this Trial Chamber has also heard evidence that Mr. Medunjanin's wife, Sadeta Medunjanin, was taken out from the Omarska camp and subsequently exhumed from a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And again, for the benefit of the Court and accused, that can be found at Exhibit P03538, pages 28 to 29; Exhibit P04855, page 23; and Exhibit P04853, page 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are aware of this, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I don't see the document. I only see that those documents are mentioned in English. I don't know about his wife. I really don't know. I can't talk about things I don't know. I can only say that I'm sorry, not only for them, but for anybody. I don't have the translation of the documents that you have just mentioned, and I heard you saying that the body of his wife was exhumed. I don't have any of the documents. I'm not aware of any of the documents. I don't know what happened, and I don't have the references to those documents translated into my own language.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, I was just citing to the evidence before this Trial Chamber and without intending to call it up. My question was: Are you aware that Sadeta Medunjanin was killed and subsequently taken from Omarska camp and subsequently exhumed? You were aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I apologise, I didn't understand your question. While you were providing your comments within that context you said that that happened. The question was not put to -- put to me that way or I didn't understand it. After what you just said, I understand. You claimed that this was established here during the trial, but I can tell you that I didn't know about that, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: You also talk about the knowledge of the defence structures, of the crimes happening in the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up P03662.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the 1st Krajina Corps Command regular combat report sent to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Army Main Staff on 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 of English and page 3 of B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the last paragraph in B/C/S. And, in English, it's the middle paragraph. And according to this document, the 1st Krajina Corps Command reported that: "After the actions in Kozarac, Kljuc and Sanski Most, some conscripts of Muslim nationality had asked to be released from their units and had expressed their dissatisfaction with the massive destruction of their towns." Sir, as it is clear from this document, the defence structures were well aware of the mass destruction of Kozarac, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Please bear with me. I'm reading. You referred to questions 7 and 8; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Let me see --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: -- I'm referring to pages 6 to 8 of your statement, sir. And questions are 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. And everything under "incidents in the indictment."

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, in the report of the command of the 1st Corps that you have shown to me, I believe that it would be wrong not to have drafted such a report, but this is a report on the situation on the ground, and it is only normal that the report was drafted. It is not normal what was happening but it is normal that a report was drafted in the way it was and that it was sent to the superior command. It's the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, that was not my question.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: -- knowledge or this information of the things that were happening on the ground. Please, please, you asked -- I apologise. You offered me to provide an answer about the state of morale and to tell you something about the system of reporting and about the state of the morale and you quoted --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: -- the place where --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I will stop you there, sir, and I will repeat my question again.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Please, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think he was coming to the question -- to the question -- to -- to -- to answer to the question you have put. Yes, please continue. But, in the future, please make your answer simpler. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tried to be simple, but I was looking for the questions that were put to me in the statement to which I answered, and the question as put to me here whether the Crisis Staffs in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they have knowledge -- or, rather, that I had knowledge that the civilian structures did that and that did they know, and so on and so forth, the system of defence I provided an answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are speaking too fast, far too fast for the interpreters to catch up. So I will ask Ms. Pelic to put her question again and if you could answer the question. Yes, Ms. Pelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question was really simple, and I would really kindly ask you to give a simple answer. This combat report of the 1st Krajina Corps shows that the defence structures were well aware of the destruction -- of the mass destruction of Kozarac; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: This report shows that -- it says so in the report but in the way you formulated your question you said something else. There were no planned activities, and that's the answer that -- that I gave. To the system of the defence, there were no planned activities. And as for what happened on the ground --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be -- I have an objection. The report says what the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska Muslim ethnicity think about the destruction. This is the position of -- so we have to be precise when putting questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't see the basis for your objection. Yes, please continue, Ms. Pelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's take a look at one more example of what the defence structures knew.
