utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up D02040.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you have in mind when you refer to "defence structures"?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I'm citing by the Defence -- evidence of the witness in his Defence statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is an extraordinary report of the 22nd Light Infantry Brigade sent to the 1st Krajina Corps command intelligence and security division. It's dated 21st of August, 1992, and type signed commander Lieutenant-Colonel Bosko Peulic. Commander Peulic reports to the 1st KK that on the 21st of August, 1992, a combined refugee convoy was moving in the direction of Travnik over Vlasic mountain. Convoy was escorted by the Prijedor and Sanski Most police. It stopped in the area of Koricanske Stijene and around 150 refugees were taken out and genocide against civilians was committed by killing them in various ways and throwing them into the river canyon." Sir, it's clear from this document that the defence structures knew that the police members participated in the Koricanske Stijene massacre, isn't it? Just yes or no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, this is a telegram stating knowledge that something had happened. But, Your Honours, would you allow me to give an explanation, because another question continues along the same lines. The questions that were put to me under 12, 13, and 14, guided me in the following way: There was no plan in the defence structures that supported that and I stand by that. Now this, what was put to me now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Ms. Pelic asked -- asked you anything about the plan. The question was whether is it clear from -- whether it's clear from this document that defence structure, which is the term you used in your statement, knew that the police members participate in Koricanske Stijene massacre. Do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not very legible, but if that is what is contained in the telegram, then that is the knowledge that they had, that that was the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, in fact, even Defence Witness Slobodan Avlijas testified in this case, transcript pages 35187 to 35188, that the entire Republika Srpska knew that this massacre had been perpetrated by members of the SJB Prijedor. Everyone knew about the Koricanske Stijene massacre; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The massacre that occurred at Koricanske Stijene, that's a fact. That happened. I don't know when people found out about it, to tell you the truth. I don't know when I found out. I don't know how much later. So that's a fact. I'm not talking about any kind of participation of mine or anything like that. I'm talking about finding out when that had happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slowly again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, contrary to your statement given to the Defence, even Milomir Stakic testified in this case as a Defence witness at transcript page 45269, and I quote: "It is a fact that crimes were committed. It is a fact that they were expelled from their homes and thereby compelled to leave the area." Mr. Stakic also agreed that "most of them left out of the fear, and so on and so forth." But the crimes that Mr. Stakic and Mr. Avlijas acknowledged, the crimes that were known to the 1st KK command, the crimes that befell the family of your colleague, those are all things that escaped your attention and you didn't know about them, according to your statement given to the Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pelic, did the witness deny that there was any crime?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, if could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, at page 8 of the Defence statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: After the question number 15 goes into incidents in the indictment subparagraph. And the witness claimed that he has no knowledge of the murders that allegedly happened in Prijedor municipality. And murders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Last three paragraphs, four paragraphs -- three -- three paragraphs of the Defence statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in para 15?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Under "incidents in the indictment." Attachment A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is: How is that contrary to - page 49, line 24 -- how are these documents contrary to the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you ask the witness whether he knew the massacre at Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I may answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, massacre of Koricanske Stijene is included in our indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Whether -- my question is whether you put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: The Defence did under murders linked to the facilities of imprisonment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no. Did you ever ask to the witness whether he knew of this massacre at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I can do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think you put it to the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: -- in 1992, were you aware of the Koricanske Stijene massacre?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, really, when I found out about that, whether it was 1992, 1993, or 1994. I really don't know. But absolutely. I mean, I was not in this system at that moment that I had some knowledge beforehand. I think it was later on, really. At that moment, if that's the question that's being put to me, I really did not have any knowledge about that. The fact is that that happened and I'm not denying that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. -- Mr. Sipovac, you now know what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Later on, I found out. It wasn't now that I found out. I found out later. I cannot remember exactly when, but I did find out that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you mean when you say "I do not have any knowledge of murders"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question that was put to me: Did you have any knowledge. That meant at the commission of such a thing, did I know about that. I really did not know. I was not in that kind of system, and I have no reason to evade anything. Had I known --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript is not good enough. The witness said that his understanding was whether he had known at the time, whether he had knowledge at the time, that this had happened in Prijedor. It did not pertain to Koricanske Stijene. That is far away. 150 or 200 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That part is not a proper intervention. Do you have further questions, Ms. Pelic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. And then you decide when the break should be taken and when we should continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's -- it's time now to have a break, albeit short -- shortly. We'll have a break for 15 minutes. And then we'll have lunch break later on, as usual. --- Break taken at 11.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sipovac, you were asked about your position. Can you tell us how many desks there were at the VTO?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, there was a total of eight, nine, or ten employees. I'd have to do the counting yet again, name by name in order to remember. Between eight and ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were in charge of which department or desk?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about others? Were they in charge of something else?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Recruitment. The VTO worked on recruitment and mobilisation only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We really have to speak slowly and pause. So if Mr. Budimir said that you were in charge of mobilisation, whatever the interpretation may be, did he say that you were for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the answer, the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, and speak more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I was the desk officer for mobilisation. And Captain Micic was assistant chief for mobilisation. So, as for that part, where I worked, the mobilisation department, there were three or four other desk officers who worked together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In my question, lines 2, 3, 4, it is not recorded if Mr. Budimir said that you were for mobilisation, whatever he'd call you, chief, head, et cetera. Does that mean that that is correct, that within that framework, you were just for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. But I was not the chief. The question that was put to me, as I understood it, was that I was chief of the VTO. I was not chief of the VTO. I was a desk officer in the military territorial organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Becir Medunjanin? What was he before the war?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Before the war, since I knew him, I think he was the principal of the school in Kozarac. He was a professor -- or, rather, a teacher of mathematics and physics. Then, after the multi-party elections, he became secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us the following: Mobilisation was discussed here as an ongoing process and also references were made to a declaration of general mobilisation. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether that is one and the same thing; and if there's a difference, tell us what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, this is the difference: Mobilisation in terms of its extent can be full mobilisation or partially mobilisation. In terms of communication it can be general or public -- or, rather, it can be public. I mean, it can be secret too, if call-up papers are delivered in person. So the distinction in terms of the question that was put to me, there was partially mobilisation of particular war-time units. There was a request to mobilise them and that went on from the moment when it was declared. It went on in continuity until the war-time units were fully manned. On the 21st of May, there was general -- or, rather, public mobilisation because then all military-age military conscripts were duty-bound to report to military organs, so that they could be recorded as military conscripts, they could be given war-time assignments if they did not have one, and then be sent on wherever necessary, war-time units, or other duties that are in accordance with the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was included in the duties of Mr. Medunjanin? However, before that, I'd like to ask you something else. Did you know who Muhamed Cehajic was and what his duty was? And then I also have to ask you what his ethnic background would be on the basis of his name.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Muhamed Cehajic was a professor, high school teacher. After the multi-party elections, he was head of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Enes Kursumovic, did you know?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No. That name does not ring a bell at all. I cannot remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Fikret Kadiric and Sakib Besic?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Fikret Kadiric, I think he worked in the police, at the Prijedor police station that is. And Sakib was at the TO Staff. He was commander, head. Just before that, he had retired. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I find this embarrassing but I have to ask you this. Does -- do these names sound like Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, in respect of the previous questions, I said that it is very awkward to speak about ethnic background on the basis of names only. Through the records, the military records, one can see that military conscripts, once they are recorded for the first time, they should say what their ethnic affiliations is. I have already said that particular people have a particular tradition culture, customs, habits. So, for example, in the Orthodox world, if Krsta is a name, then in the Islamic world, Muhamed is a name. So then on the basis of that, you can judge the ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what would be the duty, the work of the secretary of National Defence, the post held by Mr. Becir Medunjanin, the person that you were asked about?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the duty of the secretary is, first of all, to be in charge of the organ and to carry out measures and activities that fall within the general framework of the organ -- or, rather, the Secretariat of National Defence at the time. Among other things, they were duty-bound in addition to the recruitment obligation and the planning obligation, there was the obligation to mobilise war-time units for civilian defence, Territorial Defence, units for reporting and surveillance, work obligation, and so on and so forth, as far as I can remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it his duty to carry out the constitutional and legal obligation to contribute to the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: As a supervisor in that position it was his duty to carry out these obligations that had to be in according with the law and in accordance with the constitution, so his duty was to monitor the implementation of plans and programmes in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is this legitimate military formation that he was supposed to service at the level of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: All war-time units were legitimate, if we're talking about 1991, and I am talking about 1991, up until May/June 1992. So these are war-time units, units of the Territorial Defence, units for reporting and surveillance, then units of the civilian protection, then work obligation units. So that would be manning. Now, as far as planning and manning of war-time units is concerned, that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which army?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The JNA at the time, still.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 1D16050. While we're waiting for this document -- 16050, if it was not written down correctly. 16050.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, were people treated on the basis of their religious affiliation or what they did?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the JNA or is this a general question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The part of the authorities where you had insight.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: That part, absolutely. I can give examples, too, of officers and other persons who, according to war-time assignment, were in the 43rd Motorised Brigade and in other units. And in the 43rd, I claim with certainty that that was the approach. Those who had a war-time assignment in 1990 or 1991, it doesn't matter, and who responded to call-up when mobilisation was carried out, well, in the command of the brigade itself, I'm sorry, as I've already said that I'm approaching the problem this way, but I had the records before me so I can say that with certainty. There were Croats, there were Muslims, and there were persons of other ethnic backgrounds. And I don't know if I have to mention them by name. I don't really want to hurt these people in any way, but I have their records where they, themselves, stated what their ethnic background was. The chief of the air defence system was a Croat. The operations officer who drew work maps, plans, and so on, according to the records there was a Muslim. The other operations officer for moral affairs was a Croat. In the brigade itself, in the command, there were assistant commanders who had mixed marriages. So I'm saying this with certainty, within the unit itself in 1991, according to the records, the official records, there were Croats and Muslims there during 1992. And that can be checked in the records absolutely. There was an increasing number of these units coming into the 43rd Prijedor Brigade. I claim that with full certainty and that can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please focus on this attachment to the criminal report where it says that these are the names of the organisers of the armed rebellion in Prijedor and the killing of JNA soldiers in Hambarine. Number 3, the name we see is Becir Medunjanin. Is that the same Becir Medunjanin, or were there several of them? It says here secretary of the National Defence Secretariat of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: His name is written here. Now whether he was involved in that, I mean, really, I'm taken aback by this, frankly speaking. Him being involved in that? Well, if it is stated here, then I accept it as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we know from this document what this document is about? This is an annex to what? Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Criminal report. After the killing of the soldiers in Hambarine and after it was dealt with, the criminal report was compiled. And this is an annex to the criminal report, listing the names of the persons who are responsible for that crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're tendering this page, page 1 of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it would be useful, Excellency, for you to have the document in its entirety. Because this events is very important and it is often mentioned during the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also it can show whether the basis for bringing these people in was religious affiliation or crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are -- the names do not arise from the cross. Do you have any objection to the admission of page 1 of this document, Ms. Pelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness didn't testify anything to the document except confirming the fact that what's already written and in the record read by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive the page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4231, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipovac, records were shown to you from the meetings of the Council for National Defence of the municipality. Can you tell us briefly what kind of body this was; did we establish at the beginning of the war; and, generally speaking, who regulates this matter?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The National Defence Council is an organ of the assembly, and members of the council serve on the council ex officio, president of the assembly, president of the Executive Board, secretaries of secretariats, et cetera. The secretary of that council was simultaneously the secretary of the National Defence organ, and his duty was to assess the political and security situation in the area of the municipality; and, in keeping with the situation and with the documents that had been endorsed, to issue instructions and guide-lines to various municipal agencies that implement the adopted policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You just said there was a National Defence Council, including Mr. Medunjanin, and there was also the VTO. To which authorities does the Secretariat for National Defence belong; and to which authority does the VTO belong?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: If you mean the distribution of departments, it belonged to the SDA. The secretariat belonged to the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, in the line to the top.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The secretariat was under the civilian authorities; and the VTO was under the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, that is to say, the armed forces. And the secretariat was too but along a different line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the last topic. You were shown a report of Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic about what happened at Koricanske Stijene. Were you, in view of your job or otherwise, one of those who received such reports?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No, my job did not include that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did Peulic do with the information he obtained? Did he try to cover up or to -- or did he pass it on to his superior command?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness needs to repeat his answer because there was no pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, you spoke too fast and without pausing at all. Mr. Sipovac, could you kindly repeat your answer very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Prosecutor asked me this question and when she showed me the telegram signed by Mr. Peulic, I said that I could not see exactly what it was about but I understood it was a report about something that happened on the ground, that is to say, the crime at Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was what -- what was he supposed to do? Was he covering up or was he reporting about it?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: He was reporting, which is perfectly natural in the military hierarchy. It was normal and it was his duty to report any incidents, if they were in his zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sipovac. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Sipovac. I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take the lunch break now, given the timing? Yes, we'll resume at five past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.21 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nedic. Make yourself comfortable, please. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Nedic.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. You are our president for all times, forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we both speak slowly, please, and leave a short pause between questions and answers to avoid problems for interpreters. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement and signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown in e-court 1D9664.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the left side, do you see the Serbian version of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the last page so that Mr. Nedic can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team or are there any corrections to make?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I don't think there are -- are anything -- there are any corrections to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions now, would your answers, in essence, be the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I don't think I would change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4232, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read in English a short summary of Mr. Miladin Nedic's statement. [In English] Miladin Nedic, a mining engineer, was one of the founders of the SDS in B and H. After the multi-party elections of 1990, he was elected to become the SDS representative in the BH Assembly and a member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. Later on, Mr. Nedic was elected to be a representative of the 1st Assembly of the Republika Srpska, that means continued to be a member of parliament. He was involved in the work of the party in Ozren mount from the moment it was established on the 28th of July, 1990. At the Republika Srpska Assembly session of 24th to 26th July, 1992, Mr. Nedic gave a speech that was used by the Prosecution in the case against Dr. Radovan Karadzic as an evidence that the Serbs planned to commit genocide against the Muslims. The content of this message has been twisted. Mr. Nedic was calling for a peaceful solution of the crisis in BH without the interference of others from outside the former Yugoslavia who could push the peoples in BH against each other. He never advocated the execution of Muslims. The next time Mr. Nedic addressed the Assembly, he stated clearly that he did not want a war which would enslave some and transform others in oppressors. He called for the treatment of soldiers in accordance with the military codes and the respect of a knightly warfare which is very distant from genocide. People in Ozren remained united which helped them to survive because there was no bloodshed and conflicts between them. Finally, he urged for the postponement of any discussion about borders which would create chaos among soldiers. Mr. Nedic has known Dr. Karadzic throughout the 1990-1995 period and participated in many meetings with him. Dr. Karadzic never gave any indication whatsoever of being in favour of destroying the Bosnian Muslims in whole or in part. And this is the summary. At that moment, I do not have questions for Mr. Nedic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, as you have noted, your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the -- of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have Exhibit D92, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Nedic.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, could you come closer to the microphone so that interpreters could hear you better.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So witness responded "dobar dan," but it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 40 of the English and page 39 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, we'll start by looking at the speech you made which is the main subject of your witness statement, your speech at the 17th Session. Now, towards the beginning of the speech you say: "This, which is happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina today, was planned 7- to 800 years ago in one of the world's power centres and this, which is happening today, is by no means new." And on the next page in the English, a bit later on you say: "I am against solving the situation in Bosnia in haste. We must admit that the Muslims have been planted to us as a people whose executioners we are to be." In your witness statement, you said that you were suggesting here that factors outside Yugoslavia wanted to use the Serbs to fight against the Muslims. This was based on the idea that outside factors, such as powerful European states, did not want an Islamic state to be created in Europe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: What was going on in Bosnia was not a new thing. It was a war along religious and ethnic lines. Our religions were both 7- or 800 years old, and we are not responsible for the various characteristics of these two peoples. I was in favour of reaching an agreement with the other side, a mutual agreement, without the diktat of any outsiders. It was the centres of power that put us in that position. I don't know where these centres are, but it's certainly not a new thing to divide and rule peoples. They divided us in the First World War, the Second World War, and this latest war, and I didn't want any outside interference in Bosnia between us. I wanted us to reach agreement between us, but it was not possible. We had reached an agreement with Alija Izetbegovic and we were very happy that we had reached this agreement to continue living side by side, but then it floundered, and then the worse that could happen happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, I'd like to ask you to listen very carefully to my question and to answer the question that I ask. Because, in your answer, you didn't actually answer that question. My question was: You've said in your statement that you were suggesting in this speech that factors outside Yugoslavia wanted to use the Serbs to fight against the Muslims. And my question is: This was based on the idea that outside factors did not want an Islamic state to be created in Europe. That was what was motivating those outside factors to use the Serbs to fight against the Muslims. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, it's probable that somebody did not want to see an Islamic state arise in the Balkans. And in that war nobody supported the Islamic state. Perhaps somebody from the east did, but from the west, certainly not. But we were not fighting against Muslims or Croats. We were just defending ourselves. We had not planned that war. We had believed in the army and co-operated with the army, until the very last day. And these power centres outside, they made all the decisions. And the bombing was done by -- by foreign planes, not by Islamic planes or I don't know whose.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Nedic, I'm going to ask you to please focus on my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you put -- ask the witness to read out paragraph 5 of his statement and ask what he meant. Probably he might have been confused with this minute and with his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, in your statement, you said, "I was suggesting" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you have your witness statement, Mr. Nedic? Why don't you upload his statement, Exhibit D4232, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellency, if it could be most suitable, we can give hard copy to witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that, but -- yes. Can you read aloud paragraph 5 of your statement, Mr. Nedic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The gist of my message was let's try to find a solution to avoid war, by not allowing others from outside the former Yugoslavia to interfere and push us against each other. I was suggesting that these outside factors wanted to use the Serbs to fight against the Muslims. I only had the best intentions, and I don't understand how anyone could make such a misinterpretation of my speech. I never advocated the execution of Muslims." I don't understand what's unclear here. I wanted us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just -- here comes the question from the Prosecutor. Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, you've said that it was your view that outside factors want to use Serbs to fight against the Muslims. Why did those outside factors want the Serbs to fight the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to see an Islamic state in the Balkans. Who? Who could have wanted that? Maybe Muslims themselves did. But even not all of them, because most Muslims had opted to live in that territory together with their neighbours. I don't have a problem with my own people. I have a problem with politicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear now. And you -- in this speech at the 17th Session, you said: "We are a people who have been determined to be executioners and to do someone a favour." Now, this reflects the idea that the Serbs are in a position to eliminate the Muslims through the conflict as they would thereby be doing a favour to these outside factors who don't want to see an Islamic state in the Balkans; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Whichever nation in Bosnia had disappeared, a third party would benefit; not us, but somebody outside. Because whenever people quarrel, always somebody from outside interferes and benefits from that quarrel. It's a law of life. I was in favour of sitting down together with Croats and Muslims and deciding how we are going to go on living together. I even compared us to Switzerland because we have the same kind of country with the same beautiful mountains, but we needed to find an arrangement to continue living side by side and that could be done only peacefully and not by war. And Mr. Karadzic never told us to go and take a territory with a majority Muslim population. The example is Gracanica. When a general asked for 1.000 soldiers to take Gracanica, Mr. Karadzic asked him, Why would you do that? The Muslims also have to live somewhere. That is their territory. And I understood him. And I did not provide troops to takes Gracanica. We prevented that officer who wanted to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your answer, Mr. Nedic, you said: "Whichever nation in Bosnia had disappeared, a third party would benefit." What you were saying in your speech at the 17th Session was that if the Muslim people disappeared, these outside factors who did not want an Islamic state to be created in the Balkans would benefit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement, you said you were not advocating the execution of Muslims here and that the essence of your message was to try to find a solution to avoid a war. Now, you acknowledge that at this point, late July 1992, there was, in fact, a war going on, as you state in this very speech. There was war in Bosnia at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, the primary goal of the Bosnian Serb leadership in this war was to prevent the Serbs from becoming a minority in an independent Bosnia by attaining a separate Serb state in Bosnia, a state in which Muslims and Croats would be a small minority at most; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Why a very small minority?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It was my question to you, Mr. Nedic. That was the goal of the Bosnian Serb leadership: A separate Serb state in Bosnia where the Muslims and Croats would be a small minority of the population at most. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, in the early days, we were together in a common assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we recognised Bosnia. But we wanted it to be part of Yugoslavia, and they proclaimed cessation from Yugoslavia. We wanted to go on living together with all the other nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go back to D92, page 16 of the English and page 14 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is Dr. Karadzic speaking, Mr. Nedic, and towards the bottom of the page he speaks about the importance of the Sarajevo battle-field. He says a few lines down, beginning of that paragraph: "A non-Serb state may be created on Muslim or Croat territories in western Herzegovina, in Cazinska Krajina, or in Central Bosnia. But on ethnic Serb territories, others cannot create any state, neither can the Serbs allow any state to be created against them, because they know what they experienced the last time they were in somebody else's state, and they finally know their status in the states in which they are a national minority." Now what Dr. Karadzic is saying here is that a state dominated by non-Serbs cannot encompass ethnic Serb territories, and, similarly, Serbs cannot allow any state in which they constitute a national minority; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when he says that Serbs "know what they experienced the last time they were in somebody else's state and they finally know their status in the states in which they are a national minority," he is referring to historical events where the Serbs suffered at the hands of Muslims and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I take it you agree with these sentiments that as a national minority in a Muslim or a Muslim and Croat-dominated states, the Serbs faced existential dangers. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, whenever Serbs were a minority, and whenever they were in a foreign state, they were subjected to some sort of terror or a threat of extermination. We have always faced extermination if we were in a state governed by a foreigner. And this has repeated, not only lately, this has been the case for hundreds of years.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you say: "We have always faced extermination if we were in a state governed by a foreigner." You -- you -- your view is also that you, the Serbs, faced extermination in a state governed by Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 82 of the English and page 83 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And there's an exchange here between the chairman, Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Ostojic, and Mr. Krajisnik asks: "I need an answer. Do we want Jajce, Bugojno, Tuzla, Banovici, Zepce and Zavidovici to be in Republika Srpska?" And Mr. Ostojic answers: "If a clear definition of the borders in that area is expected of me, I think that we have to commit to a strategy of a national state and not the strategy of grasping territories, because we would be repeating a historical mistake like in 1918. On such territory, do you want me to give you the numbers? In such country there would be 55 per cent Serbs; 35 per cent Muslims; and 15 per cent Croats. Through birth rate within 10 years you will loose even that percentage." Now, here, Mr. Ostojic -- this is another reference by Mr. Ostojic, this time to the need to ensure that the Bosnian Serb state does not contain too many non-Serbs; right? That would be a historical mistake?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: It would have been a historical mistake for us to take their territories and their people into our state. However, if an agreement could have been reached it would have been justified for us to live next to each other and nobody threatening anybody else. And if those who wanted to cross over to live in either the Serbian state unit or in the Muslim state unit, they would not be forbidden. That's -- that was our line of thinking. That's why we created Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 85 of the English and page 86 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Where Dr. Karadzic speaks again, and about three lines down he says: "The thirst for territories and a greater country of the late Aleksandar Karadjordjevic had cost us three million, plus their offspring which amounts to 10 million people." And about five lines down from there, he says: "Now the question is, and you have to decide as an assembly, what shall we do if they get killed on account of some river or hill and in such a way again get to have an enemy in our own country?" Now this is another reference by Dr. Karadzic from this session to the need to ensure that the Bosnian Serb state does not contain too many non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this would not have been done by force. An agreement would have to be reached to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nedic, in fact, achieving the Serb state without too many non-Serbs in it, the one sought by the Bosnian Serb leadership, involved reducing the numbers of Muslims and Croats in Serb-claimed territories by committing crimes against them, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 7 -- if we could go to page 72 of the English, page 73 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is Mr. Rajko Dukic speaking. Now, Mr. Rajko Dukic was the president of the SDS Executive Board and a member of the Main Board together with you; isn't that right, Mr. Nedic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And roughly halfway down in the English and ten lines down in the B/C/S, he begins speaking about Semberija. And he says: "As far as Semberija is concerned, we have not done anything in Semberija either, gentlemen. We do not have Semberija, let us not deceive ourselves. There are more refugee there now than before. In Semberija, there are different authorities and policies and more Muslims than there have ever been [sic] because in Semberija and Bijeljina municipality, the majority of the population is Muslims -- is Muslim," sorry, "there are 12.000 Muslims without Janje which is 10 kilometres away." And then a few lines down, he talks about what he saw in the Official Gazette. He says: "There it says that judges have been appointed to the Bijeljina court: Smajil Salbegovic, Muhamed Gluhonjic, Alida Madjar, Alija Zvizdic, and I do not know, I also found a fifth one, Alma Halibegovic. So I am asking you, gentlemen, why we expelled all judges from Vlasenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik? Will we be accused then, I hope we will not, but will these others be better there working like this? I would be ashamed and I would regret all the victims if I lived in a state in which Muslims and Muslim ideology would judge and where their justice was done." And then a few lines down he refers to in -- in Bijeljina the fact that people are sitting around in cafes drinking Turkish coffee and singing Turkish songs. And he says: "You see, our 3.500 women and children are counting their last days there. We cannot do it like that. We have to decide about that." Now, Mr. Dukic is saying here that even though Bijeljina is militarily in the hands of the Serbs at this point, we still do not have Semberija because there are too many Muslims living there; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: During the war, I passed through Bijeljina and I saw a lot of Muslims who lived there normally, although it was war time. But if this was after the war, then fine. Muslims could live normally in Bijeljina. Nobody touched them. There were some individuals who were involved in incidents, but Dr. Karadzic never asked for anybody to be ill-treated, never asked anybody to move out of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, you didn't answer my question. What Mr. Dukic is saying here is that the Serbs still don't really have Semberija because there are too many Muslims living there; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he referred to, what he meant. If the authorities were Serbs and there were too many Muslims, it really didn't mean anything, didn't mean much.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When Mr. Dukic says, "You see, our 3.500 women and children are counting their last days there," what he is saying here is that the 3.500 Serb women and children living in Bijeljina, their lives are in danger because of the number of Muslims still in Bijeljina; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At this session, Mr. Nedic, Mr. Dukic says in the speech we just looked at: "You see, our 3.500 women and children are counting their last days there." He is talking about the dangers that Serb women and children in Bijeljina face because of the number of Muslims still living there; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he had in mind. You have to ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page of the B/C/S. And this is another ten lines down or so in the English from where we left off. He talks about Birac. He says: "If we move further, there is Birac which is 100 to 108 kilometres away and has 120.000 Muslims. That is how many there were, but I hope that has at least been halved and 90.000 Serbs." Now, Birac is an area in Eastern Bosnia that includes Sekovici, Vlasenica, Srebrenica, Milici, Bratunac, and Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now when Mr. Dukic says that there are now 120.000 Muslims there but he hopes that has at least been halved, he is talking about the need to reduce the number of Muslims living in this area, an area claimed by Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before you answer. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the relevance of these line of questions as to other people's statements at the Assembly. If you look at the witness statement for Mr. Nedic, he is talking about what he intended by the speech that the Prosecution cited as evidence of genocide. What other people said, what other people intended, I don't think are relevant to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I told you that you should ask Dukic about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. French translation has only now been completed. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The -- this, of course, is the same assembly session in which Mr. Nedic spoke and, of course, the context in which he made this speech is highly relevant. I would add that Mr. Nedic is not on trial here. It's Dr. Karadzic who's alleged to have acted with other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. What the other -- what other members of that leadership were saying at this session I think is highly relevant and goes directly to the witness's claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber agrees with you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, you said that "you should ask Dukic about that." So you can't comment on his reference here to reducing the number of Muslims in Birac. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your witness statement, you said you advocated finding a solution to avoid a war with the Muslims, and earlier today you said: "I was in favour of reaching agreement with the other side." And then a little bit later you said: "I was in favour of sitting down together with Croats and Muslims and determining how we are going to go on living together." Now, in fact, at the time during the war, you made it clear that you didn't think the Serbs should be negotiating with the Muslims at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to D115, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your view during the war, Mr. Nedic, was that the Serbs should not even negotiate with the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that I ever said that or that I ever thought that. Throughout the war, all the time except [indiscernible] we would sit down and talk and negotiate and not wage war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 25 of the English and of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, this is a transcript of the 25th Assembly Session held on the 19th and 20th of January, 1993, and the discussion at this session focussed on the Vance-Owen negotiations going on in Geneva. And at the bottom of the page, you speak, and you say in the second sentence: "And I have to begin this way. Mr. Karadzic, your signature in Geneva went up in smoke even before signed, and even had you affixed it, it would have gone up in smoke. For, at the Bijeljina Assembly, we adopted the position that the Muslims represented a religious Islamic group of Turkish allegiance and South Slav provenance. In other words, we, as a people, can talk to a people, and, in future, we can talk with the Muslims only through their religious leader, the Reis-el-Ulema Jakub Selimovski. They cannot blame this on us. They, themselves, proved that they are not a nation. Everything that we offered them as a people they refused, and had they been a people, they would have accepted at least one option for us to live like human beings and like peoples. They are to blame, not us. Let them fair as God sees fit." And on the next page, you say you are in favour of negotiating with the Croats and your last words are: "Therefore, as regards this whole discussion about the Geneva negotiations, let me not belabour the point. Negotiations can only be conducted with a people, and I am not in favour of negotiations with religious sects." Now, Mr. Nedic, it's quite clear that at this session you were advocating that the Serbs should not even negotiate with the Muslims who you viewed as a religious sect unworthy of a seat at the negotiating table; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I believe that we should not negotiate with them as a people but as a religious group, they were Muslims. I did not want to exterminate anybody and I still believe that Muslims in Bosnia are Serbs' brothers in blood. And in terms of their religion, they are the Serbs' worst enemies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, you just said: "I believe that we should not negotiate with them as a people but as a religious group, they were Muslims." But you said in this -- in this speech negotiations can only be conducted with a people and I am not in favour of negotiations with religious sects. You were saying quite the opposite at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: With religious sects as a people. I negotiate with a people, and with religious sects I negotiated as with religious sects. But they did not want negotiations. They wanted their own sovereign Bosnia where I would have to tolerate the Sharia law. I lived or I have lived for 500 years under the Sharia law, and I know how it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript. [Interpretation] I'm not sure that Mr. Nedic would have anything against Sharia, but I'm sure that he would have something against Soraya, so it's not Soraya but the Sharia law. Soraya was the Iranian queen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Sharia law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you said, Mr. Nedic, "I lived or I have lived for 500 years under the Sharia law." Now, at the time, you also made clear that if your -- the area you were from, Ozren, went to the Muslim side, you'd kill yourself. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I did, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, if we could go to P1379, please. And the passage I'm looking for is page 103 of the English and page 111 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Nedic, the discussion in this session focussed on the latest peace proposal, peace proposal which involved giving up some territories around Ozren? And your speech begins with you stating that you've started your journey to this session from Ozren. And you said: "And I have to say that I was really happy to go because my fellow Ozren inhabitants asked me what I would do if it turned out that Ozren should be given to the Muslims after all. Then I would hang myself, I said - there's nothing else for me to do." Does that remind you now of the fact that you said you'd kill yourself if Ozren went to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. However, even if I said that, it would have been only normal for me to have said it. Ozren fell largely under Muslims but I didn't kill myself because Muslims did not take Ozren on their own. They were largely assisted by the NATO shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be asked to look at the first paragraph. At least the first five or six lines that are now on the screen. Can he read that? Can he read that selection?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My time -- my time is very limited. I read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She put the question and the witness answered the question. If you like to put -- for the part you can do that in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, in your statement and several times already today you reiterated the claim that you viewed -- your -- what you claim was your view at the time which was that throughout the war you thought the Serbs should sit down and negotiate and the parties should not wage war. But at the time, you, in fact, insisted that the borders that had been created by force could not be changed by the maps agreed to in the negotiations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I never recognised the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I still do not recognise the state borders that we have now, that have just been created, because this will also have to be renegotiated. The Balkans is not in order. It has been shaken. How it is going to be put in place, I don't know. I was not the one who shook it. Karadzic wasn't one either. If anybody deserves the Nobel prize for peace and humanity, it is Dr. Radovan Karadzic. During the six years that we worked together, I learnt that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to P1394, page 85 of the English and page 78 of the B/C/S, please. Should be three pages forward in the B/C/S. One more page, please. Sorry, next page in the B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now you can see this is where you begin speaking, Mr. Nedic. The passage, I wanted to direct you to is on the next page in both languages, and it begins about four lines down in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have the next page in both. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just to orient you, this is a session where the main point of discussion was the peace plan proposed by the contact group and, in particular, the maps attached to that plan. And you state: "The border on Ozren mountain has already been drawn, the graves and trenches show that border, no one can register maps there. The one who wants to make new maps on Ozren mountain will have to move those trenches, will have to move the graves." And then a few lines down you say: "Let me repeat the words from the folk poem: The meadow is my patrimony, my grandfather got it with a sword, my grandchildren will keep it with a sword." And then you say: "The suggestion is in these words, it is all clear, the maps are drawn with the graves and trenches. And those who intend to draw new ones, let there be an endless battle. Flowers will spring for some future generations. Thank you." That was the view you expressed at the time, wasn't it, Mr. Nedic? The borders at Ozren have been drawn with trenches and graves and anyone who wants to move them with negotiated maps will face an endless battle.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, if you could just repeat your answer. I don't think it was caught on record. Perhaps I'll just repeat my question, Mr. Nedic. That was the view you expressed at the time. The border --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: There's no need.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Ozren is a mountain and it's between four rivers, Bosna, Speca, Turija. Those were the borders that we held and we defended ourselves from attacks from the Muslim-Croat army. On that boundary, in that defence, hundreds of young men were killed, and people from Ozren, their graves are there, and that is that boundary that I spoke about. That boundary exists to this day, although half of Ozren had fallen. And it had fallen on the basis of the Dayton Peace Agreement. The Muslims exterminated everyone in that area, and there aren't even any bricks left. People had been expelled. My house, my property, everything was destroyed, torched. That is the effect of the Dayton Agreement and the Muslim offensive on Ozren. And also, it is the consequence of NATO bombs that destroyed the relay tower at Ozren, and five young men were killed there by a single missile fired by NATO aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Nedic, you agree, though, that despite what you've said today about being in favour of reaching a negotiated solution, what you said at the time about Ozren was that the borders had been created by trenches and graves, and anyone who wanted to move those borders by negotiated maps faced an endless battle. That was the view you expressed at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Serb people still live in Ozren. I returned to that land, although everything was destroyed, although it is in the Federation. I did not give up on my land, on the land of my forefathers and I'm never going to give up on that, and I'm never going to sell it either. Now how this will be regulated, how Bosnia will be regulated, I don't know. It hasn't been regulated yet. There is still chaos there. There is still the Vehabije there. There are all sorts of things there. Europe should help regulate this, rather than sow discord.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In lines 12 and 13, the witness said: There are still Vehabije there. Perhaps that's a problem for the interpreters. Maybe they would interpret it as Wahabists. Those are extremists from Saudi Arabia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gustafson, do you have further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Two final questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, you have stated today that you agreed that Serbs faced extermination in a state governed by Muslims. You claim that you have lived for 500 years under Sharia law. You claimed that the Muslims have exterminated everyone in the Ozren area post-Dayton. You state at the time that the Bosnian Muslims were a religious sect who should -- with whom the Serbs should not negotiate. And you said that you would kill yourself if the -- if Ozren went to the Muslim side. Now you lived and live in great fear of the Muslim people; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the 17th Session, Mr. Nedic, when you said, "We are a people who have been determined to be executioners and do someone a favour. In 100 years, we will regret each of these moves if we make a mistake," you were advocating taking the opportunity that you believed presented itself to eliminate the Muslim people, people with whom you lived in great fear, once and for all so you do not have to face these historical enemies again in 100 years. That was basically your message in that speech; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN NEDIC
utterances.text: I never advocated the extermination of the Muslim people. The only thing I hold against the Muslims as a religious group or people, whatever you wish, is that they are forcing me to have to fire at them too. That is what I find the hardest of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you have -- any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Excellency. All the documents have been admitted, and I really wouldn't want to go further on the basis of that. Thank you. I'm not going to put any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nedic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the usher could tell the witness we didn't hear anything so ... No, like -- could you tell him he could be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, what's the schedule for tomorrow, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness who is coming in, Branko Davidovic, is the last witness that we have here this week, so when we complete his testimony tomorrow, we will not have any further business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I'm a bit concerned about this -- this schedule. These days we are losing time extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've had five witnesses today, Mr. President. I don't know how much you can expect from us. We have to proof all of these witnesses, prepare for them, and when we work at this pace, sometimes we will have some extra time. I don't think we can bring any more witnesses. We brought eight witnesses this week. I really don't think we could bring any more in a week and proof them and prepare for them. So if it goes as quickly as it does, we don't have much alternative but to have some extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bear with me a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could be seated and wait a minute. Please be seated. Just -- there are some matters to deal with. What's the schedule like for next week, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have five witnesses scheduled next week as well as General Mladic. We had another witness who we hoped to bring, but we have -- had to ask for safe conduct for the witness at the last minute because when we started arranging for his travel, Victims and Witness Unit learned that he had some prohibition against entering the Schengen area, so we had to postpone his testimony, so we don't have as many witnesses next week to fill the entire week as we had hoped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that for the moment. But in the meantime, I would like you to try your best not to lose any more time in the future. Yes, would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I say something, Excellency. My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- I told the witness to take the solemn declaration, please. I'll hear from you later on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Please be seated. Make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I say one sentence in respect of the previous topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I came here in perfect health. It's no longer perfect. I authorised the medical service to sent my health bulletins to you. Our tempo of work is really terrible. I'm not 20-something any longer. I'm three times older than that. So please take that into account as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to the topic we just discussed, do you have any observation to make, Mr. Tieger? Scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't wish to pile on, Mr. President. I -- if I have the impression from my dealings with Mr. Robinson that he was or he and his team were doing less than their utmost, and I -- I -- I would have brought that forced to his attention and I would do the same with the Chamber. We're not always in agreement about the efficiency or sort of reliability of everything that is going on. Mr. Robinson knows that. But I would not suggest that when Mr. Robinson says that he and his team are straining themselves to the utmost that he is expressing anything other than what I have come to understand is -- is the case. Now I have offered some suggestions about more efficiency. I see the Trial Chamber has some urging about additional matters that could be taken. Mr. Karadzic responded to that about what their capacities may be. I think those are all factors to be taken into consideration, but I -- I have raised in a related way these sort of similar concerns of Mr. Robinson because it puts a strain on the Prosecution when everything doesn't run as smoothly as -- as possible, but Mr. Robinson has talked with me about that, and I can appreciate the struggle and the -- I believe, the sincere efforts he is making to deal with that. That's about all I can share with the Court except to say that behind the scenes, it can be an immense struggle for everyone. I will commit myself to letting the Court know if, for some reason, I think less than an optimum effort is being made by anyone, but I'm not in a position to say that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, thank you for your understanding, Mr. Davidovic. Before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, incriminate means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let us speak slowly, both of us, so that what we say can be recorded. Also, let us pause between my questions and your answers. So if you look at the cursor you will see when the interpretation is over. Have you provided my Defence team with a statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D9665 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please focus on the left-hand side of the screen. That's the Serbian version. Do you see the first page of your statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see the first page of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have read and signed that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he could identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this statement faithfully reflect what you communicated to the Defence team or would you like something to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the time being, I have no objections and I'm not asking for any corrections to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, the same as those that were put to you when this statement was taken, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my answers would basically be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender Mr. Branko Davidovic's statement into evidence according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objections, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's one associated exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. 1D9602, you do not object to the admission of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that exhibit is already admitted -- or that document, rather, is already admitted as P3663.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please check it, Mr. Robinson, and come back if it is not the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out in the English language a brief summary of Mr. Branko Davidovic's statement. [In English] Branko Davidovic responded to the mobilisation carried out by the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade in 1992 and was assigned to the post of battalion commander and soon after as the assistant of the commander of morale on the level of brigade. Before the war broke out, the interethnic relations between the Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian citizens in Sanski Most municipality were good. In the first multi-party elections in Sanski Most, the SDS got the greatest number of votes and it therefore formed the local authorities. Although there were almost as many Muslims as Serbs, the Muslims had far fewer voters because the average Muslim family has five to six children, most of whom were under voting age. At the local level, the SDA was under enormous pressure from the SDA in Sarajevo and they were -- soon revealed their political goals as being the cessation of BH from Yugoslavia and the creation of a unitary state. The local HDZ was also under pressure from the HDZ leadership in Sarajevo and the HDZ from the Republic of Croatia. The policy of the HDZ leadership immediately before the war was that Bosnia should secede from Yugoslavia, after which the parts of BH populated by Croats and the territories that mattered to the Croats were to be annexed to the Republic of Croatia. When the confrontations reached the level wanted to -- wanted by the Muslims and Croatian separatists, a referendum on the independence of BH was organised.
