The Serbs did not take part in the referendum. And in response to the memorandum of independence, Serbs organised plebiscite in which the absolute majority of Serbs and many other citizens were voted for preference to preserve the -- both peace and common state of Yugoslavia. When the responsible command assessed that the security of the state and citizens were threatened, it orders a mobilisation of the commands and units of the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade in Sanski Most. The Serbs and a small number of Muslim and Croatian citizens responded to the mobilisation. In the month of June 1991, the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade set off for the general sector of Jasenovac in Croatia. In Sanski Most municipality or in places where the Muslims and Croats were the majority population, Serbian citizens had already noticed that the Muslims and Croats were arming themselves, forming armed groups and units, and organising village guards. Due to fear, village guards were also organised in response in the places where the Serbs lived. The memory of the crimes committed against the Serbs during the Second World War contributed to increase the fear. On 2nd and 3rd of April, 1992, the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade was allowed to return to Sanski Most municipality in order to prevent interethnic conflicts. The Muslims entered by force and blockaded the municipality building in the hope of seizing power because the Serbs had won the largest numbers of seats in the municipal assembly and the president of the municipal assembly was also a Serb. Information gathered by the security services in Sanski Most revealed that many Muslims and Croats were armed and paramilitary units had already been formed, and so operative measures were taken to crack down on these developments. Appeals were made to eminent Muslim and Croatian citizens in key communities to speak to their fellow citizens and ask them to collect and surrender all illegal weapons. In order to find and disarm Muslim and Croatian paramilitary formations, groups and individuals, the units of the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade legitimately checked and searched populated places in Sanski Most municipality on the 25th of May, 1992. About ten members of Mr. Davidovic's unit were killed or wounded in the fighting around Hrustovo village. This is a clear example that there was a well-armed unit with the strength of one battalion in Hrustovo and that the brigade was not fighting unarmed civilians. The security services identified and located in their operative work individuals and groups that were illegally armed in Sanski Most municipality, and these people and those connected with them were found and arrested. In the number of suspects increased -- as the number of suspects increased and more people had to be accommodated before the interviews could take place, a remand prison was set up at the Betonirka, and reception centres were set up in the Famos sports hall and factory. People were not brought in at random and civilians were not arrested. And that is the short summary, and at that moment, I do not have questions for Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Davidovic, as you have noted, your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing. That is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. McKenna, do you like that start today or do it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands. I'm happy to do whichever Your Honour would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then let us start.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, just to begin with, a -- I'd like to clarify a preliminary point from your statement. In paragraph 1, you say that you used to be a teacher. That was a teacher at a primary school in Tomina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I taught in Donja Kamengrad and in the Narodni Front school in Sanski Most. That's where I taught school.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at paragraph 14 of your statement, you say that when you joined the 1st -- the 6th Brigade you were first assigned as the battalion commander and then you subsequently became the assistant commander for morale. We'll come onto the operations in which you were involved as a battalion commander, but I'd like to focus briefly on your role as assistant commander for morale. Now, you were responsible in this role for reporting to the 1st Krajina Corps Command on morale issues; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And on the basis of these reports, the 1st Krajina Brigade Command would report to the VRS Main Staff on the state of combat -- of morale in Sanski Most municipality. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. That was the chain of command, and that's how things should have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to look at first at the document which you assisted in drafting. That's P3663. And I'd like to focus on the English page 4 and B/C/S page 5 of this document. Now, this, Mr. Davidovic, is the part of the document in which you state in paragraph 16 of your statement that the situation is clearly presented. If we could focus towards the bottom of the page in English. And you're discussing the situation -- the Muslim leadership in Sanski Most municipality, and you state, the document states: "The documents found show that they intended to commit a genocide against the Serbian people, killed them, and expel them, and create a Muslim state in these parts. All renowned Serbs and their families were to killed and hanged in the park in Sanski Most. Serbian girls and women were to be put in brothels to bear offspring to the Mujahedin, and the Janissaries, Sharia law and government were to be introduced as in Iran. Male Serbian children were to be circumcised and brought up according to Islamic laws and principles." Now, this was the type of information that you, as assistant commander for morale, were providing your troops, was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you're just saying, this information was collected by the public security service and the public security services in the units. Based on the reports that they submitted to the authorised bodies, revealed the facts that you have just read out to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, on -- in paragraph 13 of your statement, you say that on returning to Sanski Most, the brigade installed itself in Lusci Palanka and the break -- brigade command thought that it would in this way help to calm tensions between the divided citizens. Now Colonel Branko Basara was the commander of your brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see P3660. Mr. Davidovic, this is the war-time record of the 6th Brigade written by Colonel Basara. Could we turn to page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm seeking explanation. Is this a war diary, or was this written subsequently? Is this a memoire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We dealt with this issue. Probably you raised this. But this is already admitted. But if could you help Mr. Karadzic, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I believe it's clear from the context that it was written in 1992. And it's entitled: War record of the 6th Brigade. But as Your Honour has pointed out, it is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now at -- under heading 4 in this document, Mr. -- or Colonel Basara states: "On 3rd of April, 1991, the 6th was transferred in complete order and with the utmost secrecy from Jasenovac to the area of Sanski Most so that everyone was surprised." That should be a reference to the 3rd of April, 1992, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade arrived between the 3rd and 4th of April in 1992 from the Jasenovac sector to Sanski Most municipality, i.e., to Lusci Palanka, and that place is some 25 kilometres away from Sanski Most and it is mostly inhabited by Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm going to -- sorry to interrupt you. I'm going to ask you to just listen to my questions and -- carefully and answer them as concisely as possible. And your answer to that was yes, I believe. If we look at what Colonel Basara says next, he states that: "With the arrival of the brigade on this territory, the Muslims and Croats became afraid, and the Serbs heaved a sigh of relief." So this was the reality, wasn't it? That the brigade's command didn't install itself in Lusci Palanka in order to calm tensions. It installed itself there to reassure the Serb population and to instill fear in the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. The contrary is true. If the brigade had been destroyed in an area with a Muslim population, they would have considered to be at risk and to be put under pressure by the brigade to do something that they didn't want to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you've said in paragraph 16 of your statement that the basic task of the brigade was to prevent interethnic conflicts and to secure the public property of all citizens of the municipality. Now here in this document, Colonel Basara continues: "We ordered the Serbs to arm themselves quickly and replenish the unit. Since our task as a JNA unit was to prevent conflicts between the nationalities, that is, to prevent the slaughter of the Serbian people, we could not publicly arm the Serbs." So that's the truth. The brigade's task wasn't to protect all of the population, regardless of ethnicity. The brigade's task was to protect the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At first, when the turmoil started, the brigade had the task to prevent interethnic conflicts. The brigade was armed from regular depots, according to the number of people that it was supposed to have, according to formation. People who joined the unit received personal weapons, so it didn't arm anybody else but its own members who were called up and who responded to call-ups and joined the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And on the topic of the people that responded to the call-ups, you say, in paragraph 14, that when the brigade arrived in Sanski Most, it carried out an additional mobilisation in the hope that Muslims, Croats, and Serbs would respond to the mobilisation. I'd like you to look at what Colonel Basara, your commander, said, on this topic. And it's on the same page halfway down. And he states: "We had to resort to a trick" -- excuse me, it's at page 3 of the B/C/S. Yeah. "We had to resort to a trick to make it possible for us to arm the Serbs publicly and legally. The story was devised that the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps had ordered the 6th to be promoted from a light to an infantry brigade and that it could have as many as 15 battalions but the brigade should be demobilised as soon as possible so that the Muslims and Croats would not enlist in the brigade. It was put about that as soon as mobilisation finished, it was leaving for Kupres. Then conditions were made to legally arm and form nine battalions." So, in fact, Mr. Davidovic, contrary to your statement, there was no hope that non-Serbs would respond to the mobilisation. Rather, your commander, Colonel Basara, was going do some length to actively prevent non-Serbs from joining your brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have the Serbian -- adequate Serbian page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Ms. McKenna said next -- next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... passage continues on page 4, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Partly. It was partly on this, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, can you answer the question? The question is: Contrary to your statement, there was no hope that the -- that non-Serbs would join your brigade. Rather, your brigade's commander was actively trying to prevent Muslims and Croats from joining your brigade.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document -- I can see that it is a handwritten document. I don't know whose handwriting this is. I only know that the truth of the matter was this. Muslims and Croats did not respond to call-ups, save for a very small number. And there were few of them who stayed in the unit practically until the very end of the war, and they didn't have any problems. This was probably done, I'm sure it was done in order to prevent any interethnic or conflicts as much as possible. I never heard that the brigade had 19 battalions and that it was deployed in Kupres. At one point, we had 11 battalions and, after a while, due to the age and the low level of equipment and many other reasons, the brigade reduced the number of its members to a total of six battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a good point to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn here for today and continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Davidovic, I would like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of January, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.
